name: premise

density.note: the description clause plus the trailing question, combined — not a sentence each

description: A framing claim beside a vertically centered ledger of parallel rows — a number, a term, a description, and a right-aligned note, each row colored by its own categorical hue.
purpose: Use when a deck needs to introduce an ORDERED vocabulary — a maturity ladder, a set of named stages, a ranked taxonomy — and wants one framing claim to sit beside the whole list at a glance, not one slide per term. The claim doesn't summarize the rows; it states why the ordering matters. Each row is a fixed four-part record: an index, the term, one description clause, and a short framing question or note, right-aligned. Both zones share the page's own background — unlike `split-panel`, there's no colored panel divide.

heading.description: The claim — why the ordering in the ledger matters, not a summary of it.

lede.description: One-to-two sentence framing paragraph under the claim, naming the two axes or dimensions the ledger's rows walk.

rows.description: Each row is a NUMBERED item: the term on the item's own line, then exactly two nested bullets — the description clause, then a short framing question. The ordinal is a CSS counter (never author-typed, so rows renumber on reorder) and the term bolds automatically. 3-8 rows; each is colored by its own slot in the theme's categorical palette.

skeleton:
<!-- _class: premise -->

## The claim the ledger exists to support.

One or two sentences naming the axes the rows below walk.

1. First term
   - A short clause describing it.
   - A question it answers?
2. Second term
   - A short clause describing it.
   - A question it answers?
3. Third term
   - A short clause describing it.
   - A question it answers?
sample:
<!-- _class: premise -->

## Growth is a change in thinking, not title.

Six cognitive verbs map the questions an engineer learns to ask — your level is the highest verb you reliably own, and how far that thinking travels.

1. Remember
   - Recall facts, syntax, rules.
   - How is this done?
2. Understand
   - Explain behavior and dependencies.
   - Why does it work?
3. Apply
   - Use patterns in new contexts.
   - How do I make it work here?
4. Analyze
   - Decompose across boundaries.
   - Where does it break?
5. Evaluate
   - Judge options against strategy.
   - Which option should win?
6. Create
   - Synthesize what isn't there.
   - What should exist?

whenToUse.title: An ordered vocabulary needs one overview slide
whenToUse.body: A maturity ladder, a named set of stages, a ranked taxonomy — anything with 3-8 ordered terms that deserves a single at-a-glance slide before the deck dives into each one individually.

whenToUse.title: The claim explains the ORDER, not the list
whenToUse.body: The heading + lede earn their place by saying why the ranking matters ("growth is a change in thinking, not title") — if there's nothing to claim about the ordering, a plain `list` serves better.

whenToUse.title: Every row shares the exact same four-part shape
whenToUse.body: Index, term, one clause, one right-aligned note. A row that needs more than that (a nested sub-list, a multi-sentence description) has outgrown `premise` — reach for `cards-stack` or a per-term `split-panel proof` slide instead.

antiPatterns.title: Rows with unequal structure
antiPatterns.body: Every row must carry all four segments in the same order. A row missing its trailing note, or with a two-clause description, breaks the ledger's scan rhythm — trim or pad it to match its siblings.

antiPatterns.title: More than eight rows
antiPatterns.body: The categorical palette cycles at eight; past that, split into two premise slides by group rather than repeating hues.

antiPatterns.title: The heading summarizes the rows instead of claiming something
antiPatterns.body: "Six cognitive verbs" restates the list; "growth is a change in thinking, not title" claims why the list matters. If the heading can't be argued with, it's a caption, not a premise.

related.name: split-panel
related.when: the featured element deserves its own colored panel, not a shared background

related.name: list-tabular
related.when: the rows need MORE than four fields, or a header row naming the columns

related.name: cards-stack
related.when: each term needs its own multi-sentence body, not a one-clause row

related.name: glossary
related.when: the terms are unordered and there's no claim to make about their sequence

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing the row as a nested `- Title` / `  - body` pair instead of one inline line.
commonMistakes.fix: `premise` rows are ONE line with four inline segments (code, bold, plain text, italic) — the nested title+body pattern other card-style layouts use doesn't apply here; the row parser looks for a `…` immediately followed by descriptive text and a trailing ``.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting the trailing italic note, expecting the row to still align.
commonMistakes.fix: The note's column is reserved whether or not it's authored — an empty note leaves a blank cell rather than collapsing the row, so pad it or the row reads unfinished.

dataShapeGuidance: Rows should be authored in the ranking's natural order (lowest to highest, or first to last) — the row order IS the categorical color order.
Up to eight rows are colored from the categorical palette before hues repeat; past eight, split into two slides.

stressDoc.summary: Eight rows — the categorical palette's ceiling.
stressDoc.sample:
<!-- _class: premise -->

## Eight is where one palette cycle ends.

Past eight rows the categorical hues repeat, so eight is this layout's practical ceiling.

1. Novice
   - Follows a script closely.
   - Can you repeat it?
2. Advanced beginner
   - Recognizes recurring situations.
   - Have you seen this before?
3. Competent
   - Plans deliberately.
   - What's the goal here?
4. Proficient
   - Sees the whole, not just rules.
   - What does the situation call for?
5. Expert
   - Acts on intuition from experience.
   - What feels right?
6. Master
   - Refines the craft itself.
   - What could be better?
7. Practitioner
   - Teaches the craft to others.
   - How do I pass this on?
8. Steward
   - Shapes the field's standards.
   - What should the craft become?

escalateTo: split across slides (auto with autosplit: on)
capacity.note: Measured on the reflowed stack, not estimated — a graded 3..7-row render at each family size. Landscape and mobile hold 9+; SQUARE holds 6 (7 overflows by 18px) and PORTRAIT only 5 (6 by 71px), because portrait carries the largest type scale of the four. The flat block is the landscape budget; adapt.capacity tightens square and tall to what they measured. premise shipped with no capacity block at all, so an over-long ledger could neither warn nor split — it just clipped.

split.note: §0c places premise as READ-ACROSS — the rows are read against each other (a ladder), so paginating between them bare would destroy the cross-reading the layout exists for. cover-paginate leads every run with the claim as an accent cover, so each page still carries the frame the rows are read inside. perPage 4 sits under the measured tall ceiling of 5 (tools/calibrate-capacity-style graded render; portrait is the binding family because its type scale is the largest). Same recipe as its peers authority-chain, regulatory-update and statute-stack.
